article.headline: Photorealistic Volumetric Video Reaches the Browser via PlayCanvas and Gracia
article.lede: For two years, **4D Gaussian Splatting** — a technique for encoding dynamic, photo-real scenes as animated clouds of mathematical ellipsoids — existed mainly in research papers and workstation demo reels. The integration of Gracia with the open-source PlayCanvas Engine, announced on April 2, 2026, changes the delivery model: photorealistic volumetric humans and environments can now stream into any web page, no app download required.
article.body:
The foundation is *Gaussian splatting*, a rendering approach in which a scene is encoded not as triangular polygons but as millions of semi-transparent, oriented ellipsoids — each described by position, scale, rotation, color, and opacity. Because these splats can be rasterized in parallel on a GPU, the method preserves the soft edges and subsurface detail that polygon meshes flatten while still running in real time. The **4D variant**, introduced concurrently by two independent research groups at CVPR and ICLR 2024, adds a temporal dimension: each primitive carries a trajectory through time, so a single trained model can reproduce a dynamic scene — a walking figure, a billowing garment — at any requested timestamp, rather than storing a discrete frame for every moment.

**PlayCanvas** is an MIT-licensed, open-source web 3D engine with nearly 15,000 GitHub stars, built and led by CEO Will Eastcott, who previously engineered graphics at Criterion Software on *RenderWare* (the graphics middleware that powered the *Grand Theft Auto* series and hundreds of other PlayStation 2-era titles). PlayCanvas was among the first production 3D engines to ship full *WebGPU* support — the successor browser graphics API to WebGL that exposes modern GPU compute pipelines — and its SuperSplat toolchain made it a reference environment for 3D Gaussian Splat editing on the open web.

**Gracia** is a London startup founded by Georgii Vysotskii and Andrey Volodin that raised $2.9M across two rounds, the latest $1.7M in December 2025, to build what it describes as full-stack infrastructure for 4DGS. The central engineering problem was not the rendering algorithm itself but the surrounding pipeline: raw 4DGS captures weigh roughly 100 gigabytes per minute of footage. Gracia compresses that to approximately one gigabyte per minute and streams the result at 17–75 Mbps over WebGPU, directly in a browser. A frame-interpolation step lifts 30-fps captures to 90 fps by mathematically tracing splat trajectories between keyframes — a deterministic geometric calculation rather than a generative inference.

The PlayCanvas integration elevates Gracia's 4DGS streams to first-class scene objects: they support real-time relighting, shadow casting, and post-processing effects, and can be composited with ordinary polygon meshes in the same scene. A live demo and MIT-licensed sample code were published alongside the announcement. Gracia had already deployed the pipeline commercially — a Karl Kani fashion runway (the first 4DGS runway show), a four-minute music video for UK artist Amy May that reached 1.5 million views in its opening weekend, and installations at PortAventura, a European theme park. The PlayCanvas integration shifts that capability from proprietary player contracts to any developer using the free engine.

The broader implication is distributional. *Volumetric video* — capturing real performers as three-dimensional objects rather than flat rectangles — has been a commercial promise for roughly a decade, stranded behind expensive multi-camera rigs and enormous file sizes. 4DGS does not eliminate the capture hardware requirement, but it compresses the display cost dramatically, and browser-native delivery removes the final gating factor: the viewer's platform. The technique arrives precisely as WebGPU reaches mainstream browser support, suggesting the infrastructure conditions for this class of content are finally converging.

concepts.definition: An extension of 3D Gaussian Splatting into the time domain. Each scene element is represented as an ellipsoid with a trajectory through both space and time, letting a single trained model reconstruct dynamic scenes — moving people, flowing fabric — at arbitrary timestamps. Two independent research groups published the foundational technique concurrently at CVPR and ICLR 2024.

A real-time 3D scene representation in which geometry and appearance are encoded as millions of semi-transparent, oriented Gaussian ellipsoids (splats) rather than polygon meshes. Each splat stores position, scale, rotation, color, and opacity; they are rasterized in parallel on the GPU, enabling real-time photorealistic rendering of scenes reconstructed from photographs or video.

The modern browser graphics API that succeeds WebGL. Where WebGL exposed a simplified view of the GPU, WebGPU provides direct access to compute shaders and modern GPU pipelines, enabling workloads — like streaming and rendering 4D Gaussian Splats — that would be impractical in older browser graphics stacks.

A capture and playback format that records real-world subjects as three-dimensional objects rather than flat 2D rectangles. Unlike conventional video, volumetric footage can be viewed from any angle in real time. Traditional approaches used dense multi-camera rigs and polygon meshes; 4D Gaussian Splatting is a newer representation that achieves higher fidelity at lower playback cost.

A cross-platform 3D graphics middleware engine developed by Criterion Software in the late 1990s and early 2000s. Licensed to hundreds of game studios, it became the dominant rendering engine of the PlayStation 2 era, underpinning titles including the Grand Theft Auto series.

PlayCanvas's open-source, browser-based editor for Gaussian Splats. It allows users to load, crop, filter, and export Gaussian Splat scenes without installing software, and serves as a key component of PlayCanvas's broader Gaussian Splatting toolchain.

A technique for synthesizing in-between frames from a lower-frame-rate source. In Gracia's pipeline, splat trajectories are mathematically interpolated between keyframes to lift 30-fps captures to 90 fps — a deterministic geometric calculation rather than a neural or generative inference.

repos.summary: The open-source PlayCanvas 3D engine, MIT-licensed, built on WebGL, WebGPU, WebXR, and glTF. One of the first production web 3D engines to ship full WebGPU support including compute shaders. Has native Gaussian Splatting rendering built in and is the runtime in which the Gracia 4DGS integration runs.

PlayCanvas's browser-based 3D Gaussian Splat editor and toolchain, MIT-licensed. Requires no installation and runs entirely in a WebGPU-capable browser. Supports 3DGS and 4DGS playback and editing, serving as the primary entry point for developers working with Gaussian Splat content in the PlayCanvas ecosystem.

The reference implementation for the CVPR 2024 paper on 4D Gaussian Splatting, from the HUSTVL Vision Lab. It encodes dynamic 3D scenes as 4D neural Gaussian fields using a decomposed HexPlane voxel encoding and a lightweight MLP for per-Gaussian deformation, achieving 82 fps at 800x800 on an RTX 3090.

poster_willeastcott.blurb: Will Eastcott is a veteran graphics programmer and co-founder of PlayCanvas, a WebGL game engine. He previously worked at Criterion Software on the RenderWare engine, contributing to Dreamcast titles. He posts about real-time graphics, WebGPU, and game development. His follower count is not publicly available due to X restrictions.
